stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD PUSHES BACK ABOVE 5% AS HAWKISH FED REPRICING CONTINUES
stories.body: Two days after the FOMC's quarter-point hike to 3.75%-4.00%, the 10-year Treasury yield climbed roughly 6 bps to 5.01%, closing out a losing week for stocks even as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 both ticked higher Friday.
stories.explain: Wednesday's initial move lower in long yields reflected skepticism that the hiking cycle would stick; today's reversal back above 5% shows that skepticism fading as the market digests Fed officials' signal that at least one more hike is likely before year-end. When investors raise their expected path of future short rates, the 10-year's pricing formula — expected average short rate plus term premium — pushes higher even without any new Fed action that day.

stories.headline: S&P 500, NASDAQ 100 EKE OUT GAINS BUT STILL POST WEEKLY LOSSES ON RATE JITTERS
stories.body: The S&P 500 rose 0.17% to 7,650 and the Nasdaq 100 climbed 0.67% to 29,644 on Friday, but both indexes still finished the week lower as the 10-year yield's return to 5% kept pressure on valuations.
stories.explain: A single day's bounce doesn't undo a week's worth of discount-rate math: when the rate used to value future corporate cash flows rises, present values of those cash flows fall, hitting long-duration growth stocks hardest. Friday's modest gain reflects some dip-buying and short-covering, but the weekly net loss shows the market still repricing for a Fed that means what it said about more hikes.

stories.headline: WTI FALLS THIRD STRAIGHT SESSION TO $100 AS SAUDI PIPELINE FEARS EASE
stories.body: WTI crude dropped 1.6% to roughly $100 a barrel while Brent slipped 0.9% to about $103.87, with both benchmarks finishing the week essentially flat as traders concluded Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline outage will dent supply less than first feared.
stories.explain: WTI and Brent are priced off different supply pools — WTI off U.S. domestic inventories and pipeline flows, Brent off seaborne international cargoes more exposed to Middle East disruptions. The narrowing spread here reflects the market unwinding its initial fear premium: if the pipeline outage reroutes rather than removes barrels from the global market, the risk discount priced into Brent has less reason to persist.

stories.headline: GOLD HITS WEEKLY HIGH NEAR $4,400 AS FALLING OIL COOLS INFLATION EXPECTATIONS
stories.body: Gold rallied about 1.1% to roughly $4,391 an ounce, touching a weekly high near $4,440 intraday, even as nominal Treasury yields ticked higher — a sign investors read this week's oil pullback as taking pressure off the inflation outlook.
stories.explain: Gold is priced off real (inflation-adjusted) yields, not nominal ones, so nominal yields and gold can move in the same direction when inflation expectations fall faster than nominal rates rise. A third straight down session for crude lowers near-term breakeven inflation pricing (the gap between nominal and TIPS yields), which can pull real yields down or flat even while the nominal 10-year pushes back above 5% on Fed-hike repricing.

stories.headline: DOLLAR INDEX HOLDS FLAT NEAR 100.21 AS TRADERS AWAIT NEXT INFLATION PRINT
stories.body: The DXY was essentially unchanged at 100.21, down 0.02%, consolidating just above the psychological 100 level as this week's hawkish Fed hike is already largely priced in.
stories.explain: A currency's level reflects the market's expected interest-rate differential against other major economies over the relevant horizon, not just the most recent policy headline, so a flat DXY here means Wednesday's hike surprise has already been absorbed into forward pricing. Next week's core PCE print is the next real catalyst: a hot number would reinforce the case for another hike and likely push the dollar higher, while a soft one could undercut it.

stories.headline: DUKE TOPS PRESEASON POWER 44 AS ARIZONA, FRESH OFF FINAL FOUR RUN, LOOMS AS CHALLENGER
stories.body: Duke opened at No. 1 in Andy Katz's first Power 44 rankings for the 2026-27 season, with Arizona — coming off a 36-win season and the program's first Final Four appearance since 2001 — carrying championship expectations into a Midnight Madness event at McKale Center on Sept. 26.

stories.headline: PISTONS LOCK UP AUSAR THOMPSON ON 5-YEAR, $155M EXTENSION, TURNING UP HEAT ON JALEN DUREN STALEMATE
stories.body: Detroit and Thompson agreed to a fully guaranteed five-year, $155 million rookie-scale extension a day after his All-Defensive First Team season, immediately intensifying pressure on the Pistons to resolve their months-long contract standoff with restricted free agent center Jalen Duren before his Oct. 1 qualifying-offer deadline.

stories.headline: VIKINGS QB KYLER MURRAY RULED OUT VS. BEARS WITH CONCUSSION, CARSON WENTZ TO START
stories.body: Murray will miss Sunday's divisional matchup after suffering a concussion in Minnesota's Week 1 game, handing the start to veteran Carson Wentz as the Vikings open Week 2 shorthanded at their most important position.

stories.headline: VANDERBILT STUNS NC STATE 35-31 ON FUMBLE-RETURN TD WITH ONE SECOND LEFT
stories.body: Trailing by 17 at one point, Vanderbilt completed the comeback when Wolfpack QB CJ Bailey tried to run out the clock from his own 5-yard line on fourth down, fumbled while being tackled, and Cayden Daniels scooped it up for the game-winning touchdown as time expired.

deepDive.title: The Game Theory of NBA Restricted Free Agency: Why Ausar Thompson Signed and Jalen Duren Hasn't
content: Detroit closed out the same week two very different ways with its young frontcourt. Ausar Thompson, coming off an All-Defensive First Team season, signed a fully guaranteed five-year, $155 million rookie-scale extension without much drama. Jalen Duren, a restricted free agent since July, remains unsigned, with Detroit's roughly $190 million offer still short of his $200 million-plus ask and an Oct. 1 deadline looming on his $9.6 million qualifying offer. Both are young, productive Pistons big men the front office wants to keep. The gap in outcomes isn't about talent — it's about which negotiating mechanism each player's contract situation runs through.

Thompson's deal is a rookie-scale extension: a bilateral negotiation between Detroit and Thompson alone, capped at a percentage of the salary cap set by his "starter criteria" and All-NBA/Defensive-team credentials, with no other team allowed to bid. Duren's restricted free agency works differently — he's technically free to sign an offer sheet with any team, and Detroit then gets 48 hours to match it dollar-for-dollar and keep him. In theory that gives Duren leverage: a rival team's offer forces Detroit's hand. In practice, rival teams rarely extend offer sheets to restricted free agents at all, because the incumbent team holds all the matching power and the bidder risks tying up cap space for nothing.

This is the textbook "hold-up problem" from contract theory: restricted free agency looks like it creates a bidding market, but the matching right makes outside offers a bad bet for everyone except the incumbent, so genuine competing bids are rare. That structurally suppresses the restricted free agent's leverage relative to an open market — exactly why Duren's stalemate has dragged since July instead of resolving with a rival offer sheet forcing Detroit's hand. Otto Porter's 2017 restricted free agency, where the Nets' four-year, $106 million offer sheet was one of the few real tests of a match in the modern cap era, is the exception that proves how uncommon this leverage actually is.

That's what makes Duren's Oct. 1 deadline the real pressure point to watch, not a fresh offer sheet from another team. If no extension is reached, Duren's most realistic alternative is accepting the one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer — which keeps him with Detroit for 2026-27 but makes him an unrestricted free agent next summer, flipping the leverage entirely into his hands a year later. Thompson's clean extension removes one comparable from the market; if Duren's camp reads it as Detroit's spending ceiling for the frontcourt, the qualifying-offer path becomes more likely, and this stalemate becomes next summer's headline instead of this one's.
